definition: Anguish means extreme sadness or torment of the mind and heart.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word anguish. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know anguish should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The violinist watched in anguish as the auction house sold off the instrument her grandfather had carried through two wars.
Distress is milder than anguish — real trouble and real worry, but still bearable and still thinking straight.
Agony goes further than anguish — suffering at its absolute peak, whether of the body or the mind.

Torment is suffering that feels inflicted and drawn out, as if a tormentor kept turning the screw. Anguish is the crushing state itself — extreme grief or dread gripping the whole person — and it needs no tormentor. A hostage endures torment; a parent outside the operating room feels anguish.

Heartache is the gentler, lasting ache of loss or longing — an ache a person can carry for years while life goes on. Anguish is violent by comparison: torment of the mind and heart that will not be ignored. Heartache lingers quietly; anguish overwhelms.

Anguish is far stronger than 'sadness' or 'worry.' It comes from a root meaning a choking squeeze, and that is what it names: suffering so extreme it grips the whole person.
Save it for torment, not disappointment.
Anguish is a heavyweight — save it for suffering that torments: a parent's anguish, anguish over a diagnosis.
For everyday sorrow, 'distress' or 'heartache' is truer.
Its neighbor agony leans physical; anguish lives mostly in the mind and heart.
And unlike its unit-mate aggrieved, anguish makes no claim about injustice — it is pure pain.

Its early pages are all routine — oil levels, wind speed, the mail boat's schedule.
'Boats visible on the rocks.
God forgive the sea.' Historians describe the final page as an hour of anguish compressed into nine lines, the handwriting collapsing as the lamps of the lifeboats went out one by one.
